# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains most of the engineering behind a municipal water system. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62.4 pounds, and a column of water one foot tall exerts about 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure at its base. Every municipal water system is, at its heart, a careful negotiation with gravity—and occasionally a scheme to cheat it.

## The Fundamental Arithmetic of Elevation

Start with a simple relationship: to push water up to a given height, you need pressure proportional to that height. Engineers call the height of a water column above a given point its "head," and they measure it in feet. To lift water 100 feet, you need about 43 psi; to lift it 500 feet, you need about 217 psi. Add to this the pressure needed to actually move water through pipes (overcoming friction losses) and the pressure needed at the fixture itself—typically 20 to 80 psi at a faucet—and you have the basic budget a water system must satisfy.
